sourceDoc.text:
Transcatheter versus surgical aortic-valve replacement in high-risk patients.

BACKGROUND: The use of transcatheter aortic-valve replacement has been shown to 
reduce mortality among high-risk patients with aortic stenosis who are not 
candidates for surgical replacement. However, the two procedures have not been 
compared in a randomized trial involving high-risk patients who are still 
candidates for surgical replacement.
METHODS: At 25 centers, we randomly assigned 699 high-risk patients with severe 
aortic stenosis to undergo either transcatheter aortic-valve replacement with a 
balloon-expandable bovine pericardial valve (either a transfemoral or a 
transapical approach) or surgical replacement. The primary end point was death 
from any cause at 1 year. The primary hypothesis was that transcatheter 
replacement is not inferior to surgical replacement.
RESULTS: The rates of death from any cause were 3.4% in the transcatheter group 
and 6.5% in the surgical group at 30 days (P=0.07) and 24.2% and 26.8%, 
respectively, at 1 year (P=0.44), a reduction of 2.6 percentage points in the 
transcatheter group (upper limit of the 95% confidence interval, 3.0 percentage 
points; predefined margin, 7.5 percentage points; P=0.001 for noninferiority). 
The rates of major stroke were 3.8% in the transcatheter group and 2.1% in the 
surgical group at 30 days (P=0.20) and 5.1% and 2.4%, respectively, at 1 year 
(P=0.07). At 30 days, major vascular complications were significantly more 
frequent with transcatheter replacement (11.0% vs. 3.2%, P<0.001); adverse 
events that were more frequent after surgical replacement included major 
bleeding (9.3% vs. 19.5%, P<0.001) and new-onset atrial fibrillation (8.6% vs. 
16.0%, P=0.006). More patients undergoing transcatheter replacement had an 
improvement in symptoms at 30 days, but by 1 year, there was not a significant 
between-group difference.
CONCLUSIONS: In high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis, transcatheter 
and surgical procedures for aortic-valve replacement were associated with 
similar rates of survival at 1 year, although there were important differences 
in periprocedural risks. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; Clinical Trials.gov 
number, NCT00530894.).

recordedTake.finding: Transcatheter and surgical valve replacement gave similar one-year survival in high-risk aortic stenosis, with significantly more vascular complications but less bleeding and new atrial fibrillation after the transcatheter approach.
recordedTake.designCaution: The trial was funded by the device manufacturer and tested non-inferiority on mortality, and the symptom benefit seen early with the transcatheter approach did not persist at one year.
recordedTake.relevance: A landmark NEJM RCT, but cardiac rather than a vascular north star; the access-site vascular complication signal is only tangentially relevant to your endovascular practice.

check.reason: The claim states transcatheter approach had 'less bleeding and new atrial fibrillation,' but the snippet clearly shows surgical replacement had significantly MORE major bleeding (19.5% vs. 9.3%) and MORE new-onset atrial fibrillation (16.0% vs. 8.6%), meaning transcatheter had LESS of these complications, which reverses the direction of comparison as stated in the claim.

cautionCheck.reason: The snippet explicitly states the trial was funded by Edwards Lifesciences (device manufacturer), tested a non-inferiority hypothesis on mortality at 1 year, and notes 'More patients undergoing transcatheter replacement had an improvement in symptoms at 30 days, but by 1 year, there was not a significant between-group difference,' supporting all elements of the design caution.
